title: Qualitative methods and the class practicals
summary: Observations, interviews, focus groups, surveys and case studies; credibility and transferability; and the four class practicals.

keyterms.definition: Observing behaviour in its natural setting without interfering.
Participants do not know they are being observed.
The researcher joins the group being observed.
An interview with a guide of questions but flexibility to follow up answers.
A group interview of several people, led by a moderator, using group interaction to explore a topic.
A set of written questions, open or closed, used to collect self-report data.
In-depth study of one person, group or event using several methods.
In qualitative research: how far findings truly reflect participants' experiences.
Using several methods, researchers or data sources to check findings and increase credibility.
The researcher reflecting on how their own background and assumptions might shape the research.
How far qualitative findings can be applied to other settings or groups.
Coding qualitative data and grouping codes into themes.

questions.prompt: A researcher secretly joins an online group to observe it. This is:
questions.explanation: The researcher is part of the group and members do not know they are observed; this raises consent issues.

questions.prompt: Which interview type best balances comparability with the chance to explore unexpected answers?
questions.explanation: A semi-structured interview uses a guide but allows follow-up questions.

questions.statement: Covert observation reduces participant reactivity but raises ethical issues about consent.
questions.explanation: People behave naturally when unaware, but they cannot consent.

questions.statement: Closed questions produce mainly qualitative data.
questions.explanation: Closed questions (e.g. rating scales) produce quantitative data; open questions produce qualitative data.

questions.text: A group interview where participants discuss a topic together is a ___ group.
questions.explanation: Group interaction can reveal shared views, but dominant members can bias it.

questions.text: An in-depth study of one individual using several methods is a ___ study.
questions.explanation: HM is a famous example.

questions.prompt: Match each class practical method to the context usually suggested for it.
questions.explanation: Each context has a recommended class practical, though schools may change the pairings.

questions.prompt: A weakness of focus groups is that:
options: Some members may dominate or conform to others
questions.explanation: Group dynamics can bias what individuals say.

questions.prompt: Which is a strength of case studies?
options: Rich, detailed data about rare cases
questions.explanation: Case studies can reveal things that experiments cannot, but are hard to generalize.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of carrying out a semi-structured interview.
questions.explanation: Transcripts are then coded, e.g. with thematic analysis.

questions.prompt: Two researchers independently code the same interview transcripts and compare themes. This is:
questions.explanation: Using more than one researcher checks consistency and increases credibility.

questions.prompt: A researcher writes about how her own experience of migration may have shaped her interview questions. This is:
questions.explanation: Reflexivity helps identify and reduce researcher bias.

questions.statement: Qualitative researchers usually talk about transferability rather than statistical generalization.
questions.explanation: Readers judge whether rich descriptions fit other settings.

questions.statement: Triangulation means using exactly three participants.
questions.explanation: Triangulation is using several methods, data sources or researchers to cross-check findings.

questions.text: Coding transcripts and grouping the codes into themes is called ___ analysis.
questions.explanation: Thematic analysis is common for interview and focus group data.

questions.text: Checking findings with participants to see if they recognise them is called member ___.
questions.explanation: Member checking supports credibility.

questions.prompt: Match each quality criterion to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are the qualitative counterparts of validity and generalizability.

questions.prompt: Which provides the strongest support for credibility in an interview study?
options: A single interviewer with no notes
Method and researcher triangulation plus member checking
questions.explanation: Multiple checks reduce bias and confirm interpretations.

questions.prompt: A "thick description" of the setting and participants mainly helps:
questions.explanation: Detailed descriptions let readers judge whether findings fit their own context.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of thematic analysis.
questions.explanation: Quotations show how themes are grounded in the data.
